content_voiceover: This is a starred, high-yield question on CAR-T therapy for precursor B-ALL. Four statements are given, and the correct combination is statements two and four, answer E. Statement one overstates the marrow blast threshold as fifty percent, when the real cutoff most strongly linked to worse relapse-free survival is a much lower five percent or greater marrow blast burden, so that statement is wrong. Statement two is correct, prior blinatumomab exposure alone isn't an independent risk factor, but nonresponse to blinatumomab predicts a lower complete remission rate, sixty-five versus ninety-three percent, and shorter event-free, relapse-free, and overall survival. Statement three overstates the long-term ELIANA data, so it's marked incorrect. Statement four is correct, losing B-cell aplasia within the first six months after tisagenlecleucel predicts a much lower event-free survival, under twenty percent, while losing it later, at one year, still allows a respectable seventy-five percent event-free survival. The teaching point is that B-cell aplasia acts as a surrogate marker for ongoing CAR-T persistence and disease control.
keypoints: High marrow disease burden threshold is >=5% blasts, not 50%
Blinatumomab nonresponse (not mere exposure) predicts worse CAR-T outcomes
Early loss of B-cell aplasia (<6mo) = high relapse risk, EFS <20%
Losing B-cell aplasia at 1 year still allows ~75% EFS
keypoint_voiceover: Key CAR-T pearls, bone marrow blast burden of five percent or more, not fifty percent, is the real threshold for worse outcomes. Blinatumomab nonresponse, not just prior exposure, predicts worse CAR-T results. And B-cell aplasia duration matters, losing it within six months signals early CAR-T failure and low event-free survival, while losing it at one year still carries a good prognosis.
